description: Literature, ancient history, yoga, political history, biology, transport, Orwell, art, music and philosophy lead into later questions on airships, cryptozoology, geography and Shakespearean language within the same broadcaster season.

s08e01.description: Milton’s Paradise Lost lends the episode biblical scale and literary weight. Poetry and culture sit among a roaming set of questions, though the title also rather neatly describes what happens to confidence whenever an unfamiliar option appears.

s08e02.description: Babylon brings the ancient world into the hot seat with one compact, resonant name. History and culture spread outward from it through a typically eclectic ladder, where several millennia of human knowledge are treated as reasonable revision material.

s08e03.description: Yoga contributes the wonderfully literal Downward Facing Dog. The pose gives the episode an instantly visual identity while the ladder stretches across unrelated subjects, offering considerably less relaxation than the terminology might suggest.

s08e04.description: ‘Black Power’ gives the episode a charged piece of twentieth-century political and cultural history. The question ladder moves through broader knowledge while one short phrase carries far more historical context than its two words initially reveal.

s08e05.description: Parthenogenesis gives biology one of the catalogue’s finest technical words. Reproduction without fertilisation becomes legitimate prime-time trivia, surrounded by a question set that makes ordinary human memory feel unnecessarily complicated by comparison.

s08e06.description: Grand Central Station brings New York scale and railway grandeur into the episode. Architecture, transport and cultural geography meet a wider ladder that makes one of the world’s busiest terminals seem almost calm by comparison.

s08e07.description: Room 101 turns Orwellian dread into an unusually tidy episode title. Literature and popular culture merge around a phrase that escaped its novel and entered everyday language, exactly the kind of transformation quiz writers adore.

s08e08.description: Canaletto gives Venetian art a crisp single-name identity on the ladder. Painting and cultural history join the wider trivia mix, with the episode asking viewers to distinguish genuine familiarity from that dangerous museum-grade feeling of ‘I’ve seen this somewhere’.

s08e09.description: ‘O Sole Mio’ brings one of Italy’s most recognisable melodies into the quiz. Music and cultural knowledge share the episode with unrelated trivia, proving a tune can be instantly familiar while every factual detail around it remains negotiable.

s08e10.description: Sartre contributes the gloriously cheerful observation that hell is other people. Philosophy and literature give the episode a memorable sting while the rest of the ladder offers its own less existential but equally effective forms of discomfort.

s08e11.description: The Hindenburg brings airship history and catastrophe into the question set with unavoidable dramatic weight. The rest of the ladder ranges more quietly, but few subjects can match a giant zeppelin for immediate visual identity.

s08e12.description: The Patterson-Gimlin film drags Bigfoot into the respectable surroundings of a prime-time quiz. Cryptozoology and cultural history make a wonderfully strange stop on a ladder otherwise pretending that human knowledge has sensible boundaries.

s08e13.description: Tango and Tonga form a pleasingly improbable pair in the episode’s standout question. Similar sounds, very different meanings, and exactly the sort of linguistic-geographical collision that makes multiple choice feel less helpful than advertised.

s08e14.description: ‘Method in my madness’ gives the episode a Shakespearean phrase with suspicious relevance to quiz strategy. Language and culture mingle with the wider ladder while apparently chaotic thinking occasionally reveals a plan underneath.
